title: You Keep Saying You’re Too Busy for God as Though Your Calendar Filled Itself.
paragraphs:
You Keep Saying You’re Too Busy for God as Though Your Calendar Filled Itself.
Maybe the most dangerous thing on your schedule is not what you are doing—but how long you have been using everything you are doing to avoid the One your soul was made for.
Before your feet touched the floor, your hand found your phone.

Children needing you. Parents needing you. Customers waiting. Laundry multiplying. Groceries running low. A meeting you forgot about. An email marked urgent. Another problem that somehow became yours.
And somewhere beneath all that noise was a quieter thought.
I need to spend some real time with God.
But things never quite settle down, do they?
Then one day you realize something frightening.
You have found time for almost everything except the One who gave you the time.
That is what makes this so uncomfortable.

This is not necessarily the story of someone who has rejected Christianity. It may be the story of someone who believes in Christ, goes to church, serves people, works hard, loves family, carries enormous responsibilities—and has slowly allowed the urgent to consume the eternal.
If that sounds painfully familiar, there is a house in Luke 10 you need to walk into.
And one of them is very, very busy.
Martha welcomed Jesus into her home.
Martha was not an atheist trying to remove Christ from her house. She was the woman who received Him.
Then Luke tells us about her sister Mary.
Mary sat at Jesus' feet and listened to His word.
The King James Version gives us a haunting expression:
“But Martha was cumbered about much serving.”
That word “cumbered” translates the Greek verb περισπάω — perispaō, carrying the sense of being pulled or distracted away.
That is where this passage becomes frighteningly relevant.
Sometimes the thing pulling you away from Jesus is not rebellion.
Sometimes it is building something worthwhile.
Sometimes it is trying to keep everybody else from falling apart.
Sometimes good things become spiritually dangerous not because they became evil, but because they became ultimate.
Martha is working while Mary is listening.
Eventually the pressure inside Martha spills out.
“Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone?”
Listen carefully to what exhaustion has done.
She is no longer merely frustrated with Mary.
Have you ever reached that place?
And somewhere between exhaustion and resentment, your prayer changes.
Sometimes we become so consumed with what we think Jesus should be doing about our circumstances that we stop listening to what Jesus is saying to our souls.
“Thou art careful and troubled about many things.”
The Greek of Luke 10:41 contains two words worth slowing down for:
You are disturbed, troubled, in turmoil.
Then Jesus brings everything down to one devastatingly simple reality:
ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία — henos de estin chreia.
Mary had chosen the good portion.
And Jesus said it would not be taken from her.
Notice the word that should confront every chronically distracted Christian:
And that brings us uncomfortably close to our calendars.
Because while some demands truly are outside our control, not everything filling our days arrived there without our participation.
Another commitment we were afraid to decline.
Another thirty minutes disappearing into a screen.
And then we look at the Bible on the table and say:

Sometimes that statement is completely understandable. Emergencies happen. Newborns wake through the night. Caregivers become exhausted. People work multiple jobs. Illness interrupts routines. Grief can leave a person barely functioning. Scripture gives us no warrant to shame exhausted people for circumstances they cannot control.
But sometimes “I didn't have time” really means:
“I gave the time to something else.”
Because your calendar did not entirely fill itself.
And eventually our calendars can become brutally honest witnesses to what receives our attention.
This does not mean that the number of minutes in a devotional determines how much God loves you.
The Gospel is not a time-management system.
You are not saved because you maintained a perfect morning routine.
You are not justified because you completed a Bible-reading streak.
We are sinners who need something infinitely greater than improved productivity.
We need the Savior who went to the cross for sinners and rose again.
The scandal of Christianity is not that disciplined people eventually make themselves worthy of God.
It is that the Holy One came looking for the unworthy.
Jesus Christ bore sin at the cross. Forgiveness is received through Him, not purchased by religious performance.
So this is not a command to earn God's affection by squeezing another religious task between breakfast and work.
It is an invitation to ask a more intimate question:
If Christ has loved me like this...
why am I continually giving Him what remains after everything else has eaten?
We make appointments with people because they matter.
We protect deadlines because consequences matter.
We charge our phones because connection matters.
We remember meals because our bodies eventually demand them.
Yet the soul can starve quietly.
You can continue working while spiritually hungry.
While something inside you has become painfully thin.
Maybe that is why this article found you while you were rushing somewhere.
Maybe you have been saying, “I need to get back to God,” for months.
Maybe you miss the person you were when opening Scripture did not feel like another obligation.
Maybe prayer has become emergency language instead of relationship.
Maybe Jesus hears from you mainly when something breaks.
And perhaps the hardest confession is this:
You are not always too busy.
Busyness says, “There are genuinely many things demanding me.”
Distraction says, “I keep allowing lesser things to take the attention I said belonged to greater things.”
Jesus did not tell Martha that serving was evil.
That would contradict the wider witness of Scripture. Christians are called to serve, work faithfully, love their neighbors, care for households, practice hospitality, and do good.
The problem was never simply that Martha's hands were working.
The problem was what was happening to Martha's heart while she worked.
She had Jesus in the house...
and was being pulled away from Jesus by everything she thought needed doing for Jesus.
You can become so busy doing things for Christ that you stop being attentive to Christ.
You can build ministry and neglect worship.
You can serve the church and secretly become resentful.
You can write Christian posts and stop praying.
You can defend biblical truth and stop trembling before it.
You can tell everyone else to seek God while privately surviving on spiritual leftovers.
Jesus knows what has been consuming you.
He knows what must actually be done today.
He knows the mouths you have to feed.
The anxiety you have not told anybody about.
Christ is not ignorant of your burden.
But He also knows something you may have forgotten:
You need Him more than you need the illusion that everything depends upon you.
Some requests need a gracious no.
Some notifications do not deserve immediate access to your mind.
Some opportunities are not assignments from God.
Some expectations belong to other people, not to Christ.
And some moments must be reclaimed.
Not because fifteen minutes earns divine favor.
Open the Bible before opening the endless feed sometimes.
Pray before the noise takes over.
Sit quietly enough to hear Scripture confront you.
The “Jesus, I barely know how to begin again” prayer.
You do not need theatrical spirituality.
And if you have been running from Him, repentance does not mean drowning yourself in shame.
The Christ who confronted Martha is the same Christ whose grace receives sinners.
The Jesus who says “one thing is needful” is not trying to steal your life.
He is reminding you where life is found.
And maybe this is where the scandal becomes grace.
You let your Bible gather dust.
You allowed success to consume you.
Not because failure does not matter.
Because Jesus is greater than your failure.
The Gospel does not say your past disappears because it was insignificant.
The Gospel says sin can be forgiven because Christ's sacrifice was sufficient.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Maybe your scandal is not dramatic enough for anybody to gossip about.
Maybe your scandal is simply that God has been getting the leftovers of a life He gave you.
People who never physically left the house but whose hearts wandered miles away.
And when you fail, return again.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only Christian struggling to come back.
And think of one person who always says, “I've just been so busy lately.”
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Your share may reach a believer whose Bible has stayed closed for months.
It may reach the exhausted mother.
The entrepreneur quietly losing his soul inside his ambition.
The ministry worker serving everyone except their own neglected heart.
The Christian who still believes but feels frighteningly far away.
Because tomorrow will get busy again.
The responsibilities will still be waiting.
And you may need to hear again:
Not because giving money proves that you glorify God. It does not.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and financial support is only one voluntary way believers may help Gospel-centered work continue.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who has questions about Jesus.
Four words can become a prayer.
Because eventually every calendar reaches its final date.
Every achievement becomes somebody else's memory.
And when all the noise finally stops, the question will never be whether you managed to finish everything.
The question pressing upon us now is whether, amid all those many things, we kept choosing the One who cannot be taken away.
Your calendar may be full—but do not let Jesus become the appointment you keep postponing until a tomorrow you were never promised.
